prompt: What is a regression?
hint: It needs a before.

choices.text: Any defect found in the newest build
choices.why: A defect in something new is a new defect; a regression is in something that worked.

choices.text: A defect in something that used to work, brought in by a change
choices.why: Right: it worked on an earlier build and stopped.

choices.text: A fix that was rejected and sent back to the developer
choices.why: That is a failed retest, the subject of lesson 9.

choices.text: Running the failed case again after a fix
choices.why: That is the retest; regression testing runs the cases that passed.

prompt: Rui's fix for the member discount went into `discount`. Why should a tester now worry about students too?
hint: Who else does that function serve?

choices.text: Students were named in the release notes as changed
choices.why: The notes never mention students.

choices.text: Students are the most common customers of the theatre, so any change is risky for them
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson counts customers; the worry comes from the code they share.

choices.text: Every price, students' included, passes through the function that changed
choices.why: Right: shared code carries an edit made for one caller to all the others.

choices.text: The sanity check of lesson 9 failed for students
choices.why: It passed, and it never tried a student.

prompt: Match each history of a case to what its result means.
hint: Look at both builds before naming it.

pairs.left: Failed and was reported on 1.0, fails on 1.1
Tests a feature new in 1.1, and fails

pairs.right: A fix, to verify and keep

prompt: The regression run on 1.1 meets the refund of a used order, which lesson 5 reported and Rui lists as not fixed. What does Ana do with it?
hint: A report already exists.

choices.text: Records it as failing as reported, and files nothing new
choices.why: Right: a known failure is a result to record, not a second report.

choices.text: Files it again as a regression, since it failed on the new build
choices.why: It failed on 1.0 too; a regression needs a pass before.

choices.text: Removes the case, since everybody knows it fails
choices.why: The day it passes is the day somebody fixed it; that is worth seeing.

choices.text: Stops the run until Rui fixes it
choices.why: It was known before the run; nothing new stops anything.

prompt: Nobody touched boxoffice.py, but after the laptop's Python was upgraded, a case that passed last week fails. How does this lesson classify it?
hint: Something worked, and stopped.

choices.text: Not a defect, because the program did not change
choices.why: The program's behaviour changed, which is what a customer meets.

choices.text: A new defect, because the failure was never seen before
choices.why: It tests something that existed and passed; that is the regression row.

choices.text: A regression whose change was in the environment
choices.why: Right: it passed before and fails now; lesson 21 is about such environments.

choices.text: A flaw in the test case, which should not depend on the Python version
choices.why: The case is fine; the behaviour under the new Python is what changed.

prompt: Why is "retest all" rarely the regression strategy, although it is the safest?
hint: Count the days.

choices.text: It finds fewer defects than a chosen suite
choices.why: It finds at least as many; the problem is when it finishes.

choices.text: It does not fit between releases
choices.why: Right: hundreds of cases by hand do not fit in a week.

choices.text: Old cases cannot run on a new build
choices.why: Most of them can; that is what a regression suite is made of.

choices.text: The standard forbids rerunning cases that already passed
choices.why: No standard says so; rerunning them is the whole idea.

prompt: Where does the impact analysis of a release get its information?
hint: Three sources, one of them optional.

choices.text: From the test results of the previous release alone
choices.why: Results say what failed before, not what this release touched.

choices.text: From the risk grid of the test plan
choices.why: The grid says how much each area matters, not what changed.

choices.text: Release notes, the developer, and the change itself if readable
choices.why: Right: what was touched, and what depends on it.

choices.text: From the customers who report problems after the release
choices.why: That is too late: the analysis decides what to test before it ships.

prompt: Lesson 9 already checked two discount rules on 1.1. Why does the regression suite still run all eight?
hint: What did the rewrite touch?

choices.text: Eight is the minimum for a decision table
choices.why: There is no minimum; three conditions happen to make eight rules.

choices.text: Every rule goes through the rewritten function
choices.why: Right: the table is the list of what the old function handled.

choices.text: The two rules from lesson 9 could have changed since sanity ran
choices.why: The build did not change between the two runs.

choices.text: Price is risk A, so every case written for it runs on every build, whatever changed
choices.why: Risk sets how much an area is worth; here it is the change that reaches all eight.

prompt: The 1.1 suite runs no case for E, the phone layout. Which change in a later release would put E's cases back into its suite?
hint: Why was E left out?

choices.text: Another fix to the discount rule
choices.why: That moves risk A again, not the layout.

choices.text: A new account being added to the seed data
choices.why: Accounts do not change how a page is laid out.

choices.text: A change to the template every page is drawn from
choices.why: Right: E was out because no page changed; this one changes them all.

choices.text: The refund defect being fixed
choices.why: Refunds are risk C, and nothing about their fix touches the layout.

prompt: Put the 1.1 regression run in the order section 03 chose.
hint: One practical step comes before the ranking; then the ranking decides.
trap: Seats and states before prices would leave risk A for the end, the plan lesson 1 warned about.

prompt: Rules 5 to 8 fail and rules 1 to 4 pass. What does the pattern say that each failure alone does not?
hint: What do the four failing rules have in common?

choices.text: That members are charged too much
choices.why: Members without the box pass; the box is what the failures share.

choices.text: That orders of five or more are broken
choices.why: Rules 2 and 4 have five tickets and pass.

choices.text: That 1.1 ignores the Student box
choices.why: Right: every failing discount is the one the customer gets without it.

choices.text: That the run should stop and be repeated on a fresh start
choices.why: The results are consistent; repeating them adds nothing.

prompt: On 1.1, Bia, a member, ticks Student and books two Hamlet tickets at R$ 80,00 each. The page shows 10% off. What total in reais does 1.1 charge her?
hint: Two tickets, less 10%.

prompt: Why does Ana start boxoffice-1.0.py on port 8001 after the four failures?
hint: What does the word regression need?

choices.text: To check whether 1.1 started on the right port
choices.why: /health already answered on 8000.

choices.text: To show the same request worked on the build before
choices.why: Right: 50% on 1.0, 10% on 1.1, so it is a regression.

choices.text: To serve students from the old version until 1.2 arrives
choices.why: That would be a workaround for customers, not a test.

choices.text: Because the regression suite has to run on both builds in full
choices.why: Only the comparison is needed, one request on each.

prompt: Which sentence fits Ana's report of the student regression best?
hint: She found it by behaviour, and she has seen the edit.

choices.text: Rui deleted the student rule from discount, and has to put it back
choices.why: It states a cause as a fact; if the cause is elsewhere, the report is wrong.

choices.text: Student gets 10% on 1.1, 50% on 1.0; the discount rewrite may have dropped it
choices.why: Right: behaviour first, and the cause labelled as a pointer.

choices.text: Discounts may be wrong somewhere on 1.1
choices.why: Nobody could act on it: which discount, how wrong, compared with what?

choices.text: Lesson 9's sanity check missed the student discount
choices.why: True, and not a defect report: it says nothing about the product.

prompt: A case that passed on 1.0 and fails on 1.1 has found a ___.
hint: The subject of this lesson.

prompt: The theatre decides that students get 40%, and nobody updates the suite. What happens on the next run?
hint: Which result is out of date?

choices.text: Nothing, since the cases test the code and not the decision
choices.why: The expected result is the decision written down.

choices.text: Correct behaviour is reported as a defect
choices.why: Right: the cases still expect 50%, and every false report costs credibility.

choices.text: The suite skips the student rules on its own
choices.why: A suite does not know a decision changed; somebody has to tell it.

choices.text: The run finds a regression in the 40% rule
choices.why: There is no before for a rule decided today, so it cannot be one.

prompt: After 1.1, which changes belong in the regression suite? Choose every one that does.
hint: What did the release teach?

choices.text: The retest of six tickets, with seven beside it
choices.why: Right: a verified fix joins the suite so nobody loses it.

choices.text: The retest of the member booking five
choices.why: Right: the second fix, kept the same way.

choices.text: A note on rule 7 that it regressed in 1.1
choices.why: Right: a case with a history is one nobody prunes by accident.

choices.text: Removing the two cases that fail as reported
choices.why: They stay: the day they pass is news.

choices.text: Removing rules 1 to 4, since they passed
choices.why: They pass through the same function and can break next release.

prompt: Why are results kept as a grid of cases against builds?
hint: What does a regression look like on it?

choices.text: A pass turning into a fail between two columns shows a regression
choices.why: Right: each row is a case's history across builds.

choices.text: So that each case runs once and never again
choices.why: The grid exists because cases run again on every build.

choices.text: Trackers cannot store results any other way
choices.why: Lesson 18 shows tools; the grid is about comparison.

choices.text: To count how many cases each tester ran this week
choices.why: That measures people, not the product.

prompt: Release 1.2 changes only the outbox page. With the tiers of section 05, what runs?
hint: Core always; by change, what was touched.

choices.text: The eight discount rules alone, because price is risk A
choices.why: Price was not touched; the core already holds one case for it.

choices.text: The core tier, plus the sign-up and e-mail cases
choices.why: Right: the core on every build, and the cases the change reaches.

choices.text: Nothing: a page that only shows e-mails cannot break anything
choices.why: The outbox is how row D is checked at all.

choices.text: The full tier, because every release gets every case
choices.why: Full runs before a release or on a schedule, not for a one-page change.

prompt: On 1.2, rule 7 passes again but rule 3, a member booking two, now gets 0%. What is rule 3's failure?
hint: Check its column for 1.1 first.

choices.text: A known defect, since discounts already failed on 1.1
choices.why: Rule 3 passed on 1.1; a different rule failed there.

choices.text: A failed retest of the student fix
choices.why: The student fix works: rule 7 passes.

choices.text: A new defect, since nobody had tested members after 1.1
choices.why: Members were tested in 1.1 and passed.

choices.text: A regression brought in by 1.2
choices.why: Right: it passed on 1.1 and fails on 1.2, likely in the student fix.
